attempts.raw_response: Under German occupation, Welhaven maintained a firm stance of passive resistance. He refused to implement German directives and actively worked to protect Norwegian interests. Despite pressure from the collaborationist Quisling regime, Welhaven avoided any formal cooperation. His leadership in the police force became a subtle but crucial element of the Norwegian resistance, as he quietly shielded many from persecution. He also facilitated the escape of resistance members and ensured that police actions remained as non-confrontational as possible. Welhaven’s quiet defiance and his earlier destruction of surveillance archives significantly hindered German efforts to track down Norwegian dissidents. His actions during this dark period preserved the integrity of the Norwegian police and demonstrated a steadfast commitment to national sovereignty, even as the occupation imposed severe restrictions on all aspects of Norwegian life.

pair.human_continuation: Welhaven, together with Supreme Court Justice Paal Berg, Oslo mayor Trygve Nilsen and Commissioner of finance Hartmann approached the German authorities to have Quisling's government removed. This led to the establishment of the Administrative Council on 15 April and the temporary removal of Quisling's government. Welhaven was removed from his position by the Germans 23 September 1940, and replaced with the Nazi-loyal Bernhard Askvig. He was arrested by the Germans 12 September 1941 and incarcerated at the Grini concentration camp until 19 January 1943. He was transferred to Germany where he was kept in custody from 1943 to 1945, first in the Gestapo prison in Prinz-Albrecht-Straße in Berlin, and later interned in Landsberg am Lech, Bavaria with his wife Margit and daughter Gerda.
